traveler: Plato (Aristocles, son of Ariston, called Plato for the breadth of his shoulders)
title: Athens to the Grove of Academus: the Cave, the Tyrant, and the Drowned Island
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Athens: the House of Ariston and the Death of the Master

stops.name: Athens, the house of Ariston and Perictione
stops.campa: In the house of Ariston, who traces his blood to Codrus and to Poseidon, and of Perictione, sixth in descent from Solon the lawgiver, a son is born and named Aristocles for his grandfather. The wrestling-master Ariston of Argos, who teaches the boy at the palaestra, gives him instead the name that lasts: Plato, for the breadth of his shoulders, or, some say, for the breadth of his style and of his brow. He is nursed among the memory of Solon's laws and Codrus's sacrifice, a child already double-born to statecraft and to song.
suggested_refs: The Vatican and Munich Glyptothek herm-busts of Plato, copies of the Academy portrait by Silanion
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.1-4
Plato, Seventh Letter 324b (on his mother's line from Solon)

stops.name: Athens, the theatre of Dionysus, first sight of Socrates
stops.campa: A young man of twenty who has burned his tragedies to compete for the prize hears an old, snub-nosed stonemason talking under the theatre wall and never writes a verse again. The tradition remembers a dream Socrates had the night before: a cygnet on his knees that puts forth feathers all at once and flies up singing sweetly. When Plato is brought to him the next day, Socrates says he is the swan. Aristocles becomes Plato's, and Plato becomes Socrates's, for as long as the master has left to live.
suggested_refs: The Theatre of Dionysus below the Acropolis, where the young Plato is said to have competed as a tragedian
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.5
Apuleius and Aelian on Socrates's swan-dream

stops.name: Athens, the Thirty and the invitation to rule
stops.campa: When the Thirty seize the city after the long war, kinsmen of Plato's own house, Critias and Charmides among the tyrants, summon him to public life as a birthright. He fancies, like every young man of good family, that mastery of himself will mean at once a political career. Then he watches the Thirty send for aged Socrates, the most upright man of the age, to help drag off a citizen for summary death, and watches Socrates refuse at the risk of his own life. Plato's appetite for that government curdles on the spot.
stops.quote: In my youth I went through the same experience as many other men. I fancied that if, early in life, I became my own master, I should at once embark on a political career.
suggested_refs: The Seventh Letter, Plato's own political autobiography, opening its account of the Thirty Tyrants
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.6

stops.name: Athens, the King Archon's Stoa, the trial of Socrates
stops.campa: Socrates stands before five hundred and one jurors on the charge of corrupting the young and denying the city's gods, Plato among the young men crowded to hear him. Plato himself, not yet thirty, rises to speak in his teacher's defense and offers to pay a fine on his behalf; the court shouts him down before he finishes a sentence. Socrates refuses to beg, refuses exile, and names the sentence he actually deserves: maintenance in the Prytaneum, as a benefactor of Athens. He is condemned by a wider margin than he was convicted.
stops.quote: The unexamined life is not worth living for a human being.
suggested_refs: Plato's Apology of Socrates, the trial speech Plato set down as its truest record
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers II.41

stops.name: Athens, the prison by the Agora, the cup of hemlock
stops.campa: In the prison under the Agora, on the day the sacred ship returns from Delos and the city's death-sentences may again be carried out, Socrates drinks the hemlock among his weeping friends, discourses to the end on the soul's immortality, and asks only that a cock be paid to Asclepius, as for a man healed of the sickness of the body. Plato himself is absent from the room, kept away by illness, so the canon records; but it is his hand that afterward sets down every word spoken there, so that the master's death is never lost.
stops.quote: But Plato, I think, was ill.
suggested_refs: Jacques-Louis David's The Death of Socrates, painted from Plato's own account in the Phaedo
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers II.42-43

stops.name: Megara, refuge with Euclides
stops.campa: With Socrates dead and the city's mood turned dangerous for his followers, Plato and a handful of the other Socratics slip out along the coast road to Megara, to the house of Euclides, who has walked to Athens through decades of enmity between the two cities just to hear Socrates talk, and walked home again before dawn to keep the peace. Here, among logicians who will found the Megarian school on Socratic argument alone, Plato first tests, in safety, whether a single man's justice can be defended without that man alive to defend it.
suggested_refs: The Megarian school of Euclides, first refuge of the scattered Socratics
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.6
Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers II.106 (Euclides)

segments.name: The Wander-Years: Megara, the Nile, and Cyrene

stops.name: Heliopolis, among those who read the will of the gods
stops.campa: Plato crosses to Egypt to sit among the priests of Heliopolis, the City of the Sun, keepers of the oldest learning the Greeks can name. He falls ill on the journey and the priests treat him with sea-water, the remedy their medicine prescribes for a man poisoned by foreign air. Here, before instruments the Greeks do not yet possess, he watches the calendar priests reckon eclipses and the flooding of the Nile to the day, and understands for the first time how young Athens's memory is beside a register that reaches back ten thousand years.
suggested_refs: The obelisk of Senusret I, the sole standing relic of ancient Heliopolis
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.6-7
Strabo, Geography XVII.1.29 (Greek philosophers who studied at Heliopolis)

stops.name: Sais, the temple of Neith, the register of Atlantis
stops.campa: At Sais, in the temple of Neith whom the Greeks call Athena, the priests keep painted on their walls the very tale their forefathers once told Plato's own kinsman Solon: that nine thousand years before, Athens fought and beat back a great empire out of an island beyond the Pillars of Heracles, before earthquake and flood swallowed island and army both in a single day and night. The priest reminds him that the Greeks, for all their cleverness, are children who keep no long memory; Plato hears the family's old story confirmed in stone and resolves to set it down entire.
stops.quote: O Solon, Solon, you Hellenes are never anything but children, and there is not an old man among you.
suggested_refs: The temple of Neith at Sais, where the priest Sonchis is said to have told Solon the tale of Atlantis

stops.name: Cyrene, with Theodorus the mathematician
stops.campa: On the Libyan shore Plato lodges with Theodorus, the geometer who has proved the irrationality of every surd from the square root of three up to seventeen and there, for reasons he never explains, stopped. Plato sits at his diagrams in the sand, questions him on the incommensurable lines, and will later make him a character in his own dialogues, an old man teased into philosophy past his taste for it. From Cyrene, city of the physicians, the shape of the argument that mathematics is the gate to the higher learning first takes hold in him.
suggested_refs: Plato's dialogue Theaetetus, in which Theodorus of Cyrene appears as a character
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.6

segments.name: Great Greece: Tarentum and the Pythagoreans

stops.name: Tarentum, Archytas and the Pythagorean brotherhood
stops.campa: At Tarentum, greatest of the Greek cities of Italy, Plato is received by Archytas: mathematician, engineer of a wooden dove that is said to fly, and seven times elected general of a city that trusts a Pythagorean with its army. Archytas shows him the brotherhood's proof that number underlies harmony, that the string's ratios are the cosmos's own, and a form of government where philosophers hold real power without becoming tyrants. Plato leaves with a friendship that will, within three decades, save his life, and with a city in his mind's eye that Syracuse will never quite become.
suggested_refs: Archytas's wooden flying dove, reported by Aulus Gellius as the wonder of ancient Tarentum
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.6, VIII.79-83 (Archytas)

stops.name: Locri, Philolaus, Eurytus, and Timaeus of Locri
stops.campa: Down the Italian coast at Locri, a city that governs itself by the oldest written code in the Greek world, Plato seeks out Philolaus and Eurytus, Pythagoreans who teach that the cosmos is built of number set to fire, and Eurytus who pegs pebbles to outlines to show what number a shape truly is. Among the Locrian statesmen he meets one Timaeus, versed in astronomy and the harmony of the spheres, whose name and whose learning Plato will one day lend entire to the greatest of his cosmological dialogues.
suggested_refs: Plato's dialogue Timaeus, named for the Locrian Pythagorean statesman he met here
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.6, VIII.84-85 (Philolaus)
Plato, Timaeus 20a (Timaeus of Locri as speaker)

segments.name: The First Syracuse: Dionysius, Dion, and the Slave-Market of Aegina

stops.name: Syracuse, first sight of the fires of Aetna
stops.campa: Plato crosses to Sicily, drawn as much by report of Aetna's burning crater as by any court, and finds an island whose table is set twice a day and whose men, Sicilian and Italian Greek alike, gorge and drink until, he will later write, no city so fed can ever be well governed. He climbs to see the mountain smoke by daylight and glow by night, a fire fed, the Sicilians tell him, from beneath the whole island. It is his first sight of Syracuse, the greatest and unhappiest of Greek cities, where he will return three times and nearly die.
suggested_refs: Mount Aetna, whose craters drew Plato to Sicily by his own later account
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.18
Plato, Seventh Letter 326b-c (on Italian and Sicilian luxury)

stops.name: Syracuse, the court of Dionysius I, 'and you like a tyrant'
stops.campa: Brought before the tyrant Dionysius the Elder, Plato is asked his opinion of tyranny and answers that the ruler's own interest is not the highest good unless he is also pre-eminent in virtue, and that the coward's life is no better than the tyrant's who fears his own guardsmen. Dionysius flares in anger: 'Your words smack of senility, old man.' Plato does not yield an inch: 'And yours smack of tyranny.' The tyrant nearly has him killed on the spot; only Dion's pleading spares him, but the debt of the insult is entered, and the account will fall due.
stops.quote: You talk like an old dotard. — And you like a tyrant.
stops.quote_source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.18
suggested_refs: Diogenes Laertius's Life of Plato, sole record of the exchange with Dionysius I
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.18-19

stops.name: Syracuse, Dion converted to philosophy
stops.campa: Among the young men of the court, Dion, brother of the tyrant's wife, is scarcely twenty when he hears Plato speak and turns from the pleasures of Dionysius's table to a life set on virtue before self-indulgence, a stability of mind rare, Plato will later write, in one so young. He becomes at once disciple and protector, urging Plato's arguments in the tyrant's own hall and dreaming already of the philosopher's city Sicily might become under a ruler willing to be taught. Neither of them yet knows what this single friendship will cost, and win, and cost again.
stops.quote: He resolved to live for the future in a better way than the majority of Italian and Sicilian Greeks, having set his affection on virtue in preference to pleasure and self-indulgence.
suggested_refs: Plutarch's Life of Dion, the fullest ancient portrait of Plato's Syracusan disciple

stops.name: Aboard the Spartan ship, delivered to Pollis
stops.campa: The tyrant does not forgive an insult before witnesses. On some pretext of an embassy home, Dionysius arranges that Plato sail with Pollis, a Spartan envoy under secret instruction, or in outright league with him, to see that the philosopher never lands in Athens a free man. Somewhere on the crossing, in waters that answer to no city's law but the ship-captain's, Plato passes from guest to cargo: a man of sixty talents' ransom-worth, if anyone still living wishes to name a price for a friend of tyrants who has fallen out with one.
suggested_refs: The Aegean sea-lanes between Syracuse and Aegina, Pollis's chartered course
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.19-20

stops.name: Aegina, the slave-market and the jesting acquittal
stops.campa: Pollis sells Plato on the auction-block at Aegina, a city then at open war with Athens and bound by its own decree to put to death any Athenian caught setting foot on the island. Brought instead before a court on the capital charge, Plato is nearly condemned to die for the crime of having been sold there against his will, until one juror, laughing, says only that the man is a philosopher and no danger to anyone, and the court lets him go unharmed: the same wit that angered a tyrant now saves the philosopher's life among his enemies.
suggested_refs: The Temple of Aphaia on Aegina, standing above the harbor where Plato is said to have been sold
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.19-20

stops.name: Athens, ransomed by Anniceris, the garden of the Academy bought
stops.campa: Anniceris of Cyrene, a Socratic visiting Aegina and by chance no stranger to Plato, pays twenty minae and sets him free without being asked twice. When Plato's Athenian friends raise a subscription to repay him, Anniceris refuses every coin, saying Plato is not the only man worthy of such care, and the friends spend the sum instead on a small garden outside the walls, in the grove sacred to the hero Academus. Sold as a slave for speaking against tyranny, Plato comes home to find that the ransom itself has bought him the ground his school will stand on.
suggested_refs: The archaeological park of Akadimia Platonos in modern Athens, on the site of the grove Anniceris's ransom purchased
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.20
Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights II.18 (Anniceris and the ransom)

segments.name: The Grove of Academus: the Academy and the Great Myths

stops.name: Athens, the Academy founded in the grove of Academus
stops.campa: In the gymnasium named for the hero Academus, watered by the Cephisus and planted with the sacred olives of Athena, Plato opens a school unlike any before it: not a sophist's paid lecture-hall but a common life of inquiry, its members eating together and reasoning without fee. Over the gate, later ages will say, stands the warning: let no one enter here who is ignorant of geometry. Eudoxus of Cnidus, already a master astronomer, brings his own students in from Cyzicus to merge with Plato's; Speusippus his nephew, and in time Aristotle, a boy not yet born, will walk this same grove.
stops.quote: Let no one ignorant of geometry enter here.
stops.quote_source: Traditional inscription over the Academy's gate, recorded by later commentators (Tzetzes, Chiliades VIII.973)
suggested_refs: The excavated foundations of the Academy gymnasium in the Akadimia Platonos park, Athens
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.7, III.20

stops.name: Athens, the Academy, the cave and the ascent to the sun
stops.campa: Before the gathered Academy, Plato sets out the vision that will outlast every one of his arguments: prisoners chained by the neck and legs since childhood in an underground den, facing a wall on which they watch shadows thrown by a fire behind them and mistake the shadows for the whole of being. One prisoner is loosed, dragged up the steep rough ascent into the sunlight, and suffers agony in the unaccustomed light before he can look even at reflections, then shadows, then at last the sun itself, and knows it to be the cause of all he had only seen shadows of before.
stops.quote: Behold! human beings living in an underground den... here they have been from their childhood, and have their legs and necks chained so that they cannot move, and can only see before them.
suggested_refs: The Allegory of the Cave, Republic Book VII, the most copied passage of the Platonic corpus

stops.name: Athens, the Academy, the myth of Er and the choice of lives
stops.campa: Plato tells of Er, son of Armenius, a soldier left for dead on the battlefield whose body alone does not corrupt in ten days and who wakes on the pyre to report what the soul sees beyond the body: a meadow, a judgment, a spindle turning on the knees of Necessity, sirens singing one note apiece from its eight whorls, and souls of every former life choosing, in a single irrevocable moment before Lethe's plain, the pattern of a life to come. No god casts the lot; each soul indicts its own choice, and Er is sent back only to carry the report to the living.
stops.quote: Virtue is free, and as a man honours or dishonours her he will have more or less of her; the responsibility is with the chooser.
suggested_refs: The Myth of Er, closing Book X of the Republic, Plato's eschatology of the soul's choice

stops.name: Athens, the Academy, the chariot of the soul
stops.campa: Beneath the plane tree by the Ilissus where Socrates once told it to Phaedrus, and now retold beneath the olives of the Academy, Plato likens the soul to a charioteer driving a pair of winged horses: one noble, white, a lover of honor guided by word and reason alone; the other crooked, dark, deaf to the rein, dragging toward the earth. The gods' own steeds are matched and obedient, circling forever behind the rim of heaven to glimpse true being; human horses fight the ascent, and a soul that loses its feathers falls to earth and puts on a mortal body, remembering, if it remembers anything, wings.
stops.quote: Every soul is immortal. For that which is ever moving is immortal... We will liken the soul to the composite nature of a pair of winged horses and a charioteer.
suggested_refs: The Chariot Allegory of the Phaedrus, Plato's fullest myth of the soul's nature and fall

segments.name: The Second Syracuse: Dion's Summons and the Geometry of Dionysius the Younger

stops.name: Athens, the Academy, the death of Dionysius I and Dion's summons
stops.campa: Word reaches the Academy that the elder Dionysius is dead and his son, young and untried, has inherited a throne without his father's cunning. Dion writes at once, urging that the hour has come at last: let Plato cross again and set the young tyrant's soul toward philosophy while it is still unformed, and the ancient hope, older than either of them, may finally be proved in one living city, that the evils of mankind will not cease until philosophers rule or rulers philosophize.
stops.quote: There will be no cessation of evils for the sons of men, till either those who are pursuing a right and true philosophy receive sovereign power in the States, or those in power in the States by some dispensation of providence become true philosophers.
suggested_refs: The Seventh Letter's statement of the philosopher-king principle, echoed in Republic V, 473c-e

stops.name: Syracuse, the palace floor thick with the dust of diagrams
stops.campa: Plato sails a second time, and for a season the fashion sweeps the court entire: young Dionysius takes up geometry with such sudden passion that the whole palace fills with the dust of diagrams traced on sanded floors by courtiers eager to be seen thinking. Plato and Dion dare to hope the experiment is truly working, that a tyrant's heir might yet be turned philosopher-king by his own hand's practice at the compass and the line. Philistus and the old guard of the court watch the fashion with a colder eye, waiting for the dust to settle back into intrigue.
suggested_refs: Plutarch's Life of Dion, source of the anecdote of the dust-covered palace floor

stops.name: Syracuse, Dion charged with conspiracy and expelled
stops.campa: In the fourth month of Plato's stay, courtiers who fear Dion's influence persuade the young tyrant that his kinsman plots to seize the throne outright. Dionysius acts before Dion can answer the charge: he puts him aboard a small boat and expels him from Syracuse in open disgrace, confiscating his estate and, worse to Dion, his wife. Plato is kept on at court, neither prisoner nor honored guest, a hostage of sorts to his own friendship, while Dionysius courts his good opinion and shrinks from the one discipline of study that might have earned it honestly.
stops.quote: In the fourth month or thereabouts, charging Dion with conspiracy to seize the throne, Dionysios put him on board a small boat and expelled him from Syracuse with ignominy.
suggested_refs: The fortress island of Ortygia at Syracuse, seat of Dionysius's court where Dion was denounced

stops.name: Syracuse, the strained stay and the return to Athens
stops.campa: Dionysius grows only more attached to Plato and jealous of any praise given to the banished Dion, wishing to be loved and admired without the one price philosophy actually asks of a pupil: sustained, disciplined study. When it comes to that discipline he shrinks back every time. Plato, given leave at last under promise that Dion's recall will follow, sails home to the Academy empty-handed on the one point that mattered, carrying instead the first bitter proof of how far a tyrant's good will can travel without a tyrant's good habits to carry it.
stops.quote: He did become more and more attached to me, and wished me to praise him more than I praised Dion... but when confronted with the one way in which this might have been done, he shrank from coming into close and intimate relations with me as a pupil.
suggested_refs: The Seventh Letter's own account of the failed second sailing, Plato's most sustained autobiographical document

segments.name: The Third Syracuse: the Peril and the Rescue of Archytas

stops.name: Athens, reluctant, sailing on Archytas's word
stops.campa: Dionysius sends ship after ship and letter after letter swearing that Dion's recall waits only on Plato's presence at court, and Archytas, whose own name now stands as guarantor with the tyrant, urges him not to break faith with a promise so publicly made. Against the plain warning of his own experience, and over Dion's own misgivings, Plato sails a third time at sixty-six years old, telling himself that to refuse now, and be proved a coward before philosophy's one great test, would dishonor the school itself more than any danger at Syracuse could.
suggested_refs: Archytas's letters of guarantee to Dionysius II, referenced in the Seventh and Third Letters

stops.name: Syracuse, the acropolis, a guest turned virtual prisoner
stops.campa: Dion is not recalled; instead his property is sold outright and his wife given in forced marriage to another. Plato protests and is quietly confined within the walled acropolis of Ortygia, watched by mercenaries who murmur against the philosopher who has turned their pay-master's mind toward austerity, until even Dionysius admits, half in shame, that Plato's own life is no longer entirely safe at his own court. Letters go out from the fortress under close eyes; Plato waits on the one friendship strong enough to reach across the strait and pull him out.
suggested_refs: The fortress of Ortygia at Syracuse, where Plato was effectively held under guard

stops.name: Syracuse, the thirty-oared galley of Archytas
stops.campa: Plato sends word of his plight to Tarentum, and Archytas, finding some pretext of civic embassy, dispatches a thirty-oared galley under Lamiscus, one of his own citizens, who comes before Dionysius and pleads for Plato's release with the full weight of Tarentum's friendship behind him. Dionysius yields what he will not be shamed into refusing outright: he lets Plato go and pays for the passage, though not one obol of Dion's confiscated fortune is ever restored. The philosopher leaves Syracuse a third and final time, rescued not by any tyrant's virtue but by a fellow Pythagorean's oar-blades.
stops.quote: I sent to Archytes and my other friends in Taras, telling them the plight I was in. Finding some excuse for an embassy from their city, they sent a thirty-oared galley with Lamiscos, one of themselves, who came and entreated Dionysios about me.
suggested_refs: The thirty-oared galley of Tarentum, the vessel of Plato's rescue under Lamiscus

stops.name: Olympia, the meeting with Dion at the Games
stops.campa: At the Olympic festival, thronged with every Greek city, Plato finds Dion already among the crowd and gives him, at last face to face, the full account of Syracuse's betrayal: the confiscated estate, the wife married elsewhere, the friendship spent for nothing. Dion, cheered by the assembled Greeks as the man who once humbled a tyrant's court with philosophy, hears the news in public and says nothing rash there among the sacrifices and the chariot-races, but the resolve to take Syracuse by force, and not by argument, begins in him from this hour at Olympia.
suggested_refs: The sanctuary of Olympia, where Dion was publicly honored even as his private ruin was confirmed

segments.name: The Last Years: Atlantis Set Down, Dion's Fall, and the End at the Academy

stops.name: Athens, the Academy, news of Dion's landing in Sicily
stops.campa: Against Plato's own counsel, which had always set argument above the sword, Dion sails for Sicily with a small mercenary force and takes Syracuse from Dionysius in a rising the tyrant never expects. Plato, aged and remaining at the Academy, refuses to bless the campaign as his own doing though half the city credits him with training the liberator; he writes afterward that he had only ever wished Dion to free Sicily by persuading a willing ruler, never by conquest, and grieves already for a friendship now committed to a war of arms he did not choose for it.
suggested_refs: Plutarch's Life of Dion, chronicling the Sicilian expedition Plato watched from Athens

stops.name: Athens, the Academy, the Timaeus and the maker of the universe
stops.campa: In these same years Plato sets to writing the cosmology he has carried since Sais: a divine craftsman, the demiurge, looks to the eternal patterns and shapes the visible world as their best possible image, sphere within sphere, soul woven through the whole of it before body is given form. Into Timaeus's mouth he places at last the full tale the Egyptian priests confirmed to him: ancient Athens once broke an empire out of an island beyond the Pillars of Heracles, before the island sank in a single day and night beneath the sea, leaving only a shoal of mud where ships once sailed.
stops.quote: The father and maker of all this universe is past finding out; and even if we found him, to tell of him to all men would be impossible.
suggested_refs: Plato's Timaeus, the dialogue that first fixed Atlantis in writing for the West

stops.name: Athens, the Academy, the Critias breaks off unfinished
stops.campa: Plato takes up the tale again to tell it whole: Poseidon's love for the mortal Cleito, the ringed city of concentric land and water cut like a lathe's turning, the red and white and black stone of its walls, the temple roofed in silver and gold where an image of the sea-god stands so tall it touches the ceiling, the metal orichalcum flashing like fire in the hills. He brings the story to the very edge of Atlantis's fall from grace, to Zeus gathering all the gods into their holiest dwelling to judge the empire's corruption and pronounce its sentence, and there, mid-speech, the dialogue and the pen both stop.
stops.quote: Zeus, the god of gods, who rules according to law, and is able to see into such things, perceiving that an honourable race was in a woeful plight, and wanting to inflict punishment on them... collected all the gods into their most holy habitation... And when he had called them together, he spake as follows—
stops.quote_source: Plato, Critias 121b-c (the dialogue's final, unfinished sentence)
suggested_refs: The Critias, Plato's unfinished sequel to the Timaeus, breaking off mid-sentence before Zeus's judgment
sources: Plato, Critias 121c (the manuscript ends without completing Zeus's speech)

stops.name: Athens, the Academy, word of Dion's murder
stops.campa: News reaches the Academy that Callippus, an Athenian who once sat among Plato's own students, has had Zacynthian mercenaries choke and stab Dion to death in his own house during a festival of Persephone, and has seized Syracuse for himself. Plato, past seventy, writes that he claims the very first right to be angered at the murderers, for they and the tyrant before them have done the greatest injury not to Dion alone but to all mankind, having cut down the one man who might have clothed Sicily's slavery in the bright garment of freedom.
stops.quote: It is I who have the best right to be angered with his murderers... For both they and he have done the greatest injury to me, and I might almost say to all mankind, they by slaying the man that was willing to act righteously.
suggested_refs: Plutarch's Life of Dion, closing chapters on the assassination by Callippus

stops.name: Athens, the Academy, the Laws left unfinished
stops.campa: In his last years, the dream of the philosopher-king set aside, Plato dictates a longer and plainer law-code for a second-best city, a Cretan colony that need never exist, prescribing everything from the drinking of wine to the rearing of unweaned infants to the punishment of impiety, as if the whole labor of Syracuse could be done again on paper where no tyrant could betray it. He does not live to give the last books their final polish; his student Philippus of Opus will be left to copy the waxed tablets into finished order after him.
suggested_refs: Plato's Laws, his longest dialogue, left in draft on wax tablets at his death
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.37

stops.name: Athens, the Academy, death at a wedding feast
stops.campa: In his eighty-first year Plato is present at a wedding feast, still writing and still teaching to the last, and dies there quietly among the company, in the first year of the hundred and eighth Olympiad. He is buried in the Academy itself, in the grove his own ransom-money once purchased, where he taught for the greater part of his life; the school he founded will outlive him by nine centuries, until an emperor closes it as a house of pagan philosophy, and the grove of Academus becomes, ever after, simply the word for a school.
stops.quote: He died, as Hermippus relates, at a wedding feast, in the first year of the hundred and eighth Olympiad, in his eighty-first year.
stops.quote_source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.2 (trans. R. D. Hicks)
suggested_refs: The traditional site of Plato's tomb within the grove of the Academy, Athens
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers III.2, III.40-45
Justinian, Codex I.11.10.2 (closure of the Athenian philosophical schools, AD 529)
